Pastoralists in the Modern World 109 We will discuss some of these changes by looking at one pastoral community – the Maasai – in some detail. The Maasai cattle herders live primarily in east Africa: 300, 000 in southern Kenya and another 150,000 in Tanzania. We will see how new laws and regulations took away their land and restricted their movement. This affected their lives in times of drought and even reshaped their social relationships. 3.1 Where have the Grazing Lands Gone? One of the problems the Maasais have faced is the continuous loss of their grazing lands. Before colonial times, Maasailand stretched over a vast area from north Kenya to the steppes of northern Tanzania. In the late nineteenth century, European imperial powers scrambled for territorial possessions in Africa, slicing up the region into different colonies. In 1885, Maasailand was cut into half with an international boundary between British Kenya and German Tanganyika. Subsequently, the best grazing lands were gradually taken over for white settlement and the Maasai were pushed into a small area in Fig.13 – Pastoral communities in Africa. The inset shows the location of the Maasais in Kenya and Tanzania. On Tanganyika Britain conquered what had been German East Africa during the First World War. In 1919 Tanganyika came under British control. It attained independence in 1961 and united with Zanzibar to form Tanzania in 1964. Reprint 2025-26

India and the Contemporary World 110 south Kenya and north Tanzania. The Maasai lost about 60 per cent of their pre-colonial lands. They were confined to an arid zone with uncertain rainfall and poor pastures. From the late nineteenth century, the British colonial government in east Africa also encouraged local peasant communities to expand cultivation. As cultivation expanded, pasturelands were turned into cultivated fields. In pre-colonial times, the Maasai pastoralists had dominated their agricultural neighbours both economically and politically. By the end of colonial rule the situation had reversed. Large areas of grazing land were also turned into game reserves like the Maasai Mara and Samburu National Park in Kenya and Serengeti Park in Tanzania. Pastoralists were not allowed to enter these reserves; they could neither hunt animals nor graze their herds in these areas. Very often these reserves were in areas that had traditionally been regular grazing grounds for Maasai herds. The Serengeti National Park, for instance, was created over 14,760 km. of Maasai grazing land. Fig.14 – Without grass, livestock (cattle, goats and sheep) are malnourished, which means less food available for families and their children. The areas hardest hit by drought and food shortage  are in the vicinity of Amboseli National Park, which last year generated approximately 240 million Kenyan Shillings (estimated $3.5 million US) from tourism. In addition, the Kilimanjaro Water Project cuts through the communities of this area but the villagers are barred from using the water for irrigation or for livestock.Courtesy: The Massai Association. Reprint 2025-26

Pastoralists in the Modern World 111 Source E Pastoral communities elsewhere in Africa faced similar problems. In Namibia, in south-west Africa, the Kaokoland herders traditionally moved between Kaokoland and nearby Ovamboland, and they sold skin, meat and other trade products in neighbouring markets. All this was stopped with the new system of territorial boundaries that restricted movements between regions. The nomadic cattle herders of Kaokoland in Namibia complained: ‘We have difficulty. We cry. We are imprisoned. We do not know why we are locked up. We are in jail. We have no place to live … We cannot get meat from the south … Our sleeping skins cannot be sent out … Ovamboland is closed for us. We lived in Ovamboland for a long time. We want to take our cattle there, also our sheep and goats. The borders are closed. The borders press us heavily. We cannot live.’ Statement of Kaokoland herders, Namibia, 1949. Quoted in Michael Bollig, ‘The colonial encapsulation of the north western Namibian pastoral economy’, Africa 68 (4), 1998. Fig.15 – The title Maasai derives from the word Maa. Maa-sai means 'My People'. The Maasai are traditionally nomadic and pastoral people who depend on milk and meat for subsistence. High temperatures combine with low rainfall to create conditions which are dry, dusty, and extremely hot. Drought conditions are common in this semi-arid land of equatorial heat. During such times pastoral animals die in large numbes. Courtesy: The Massai Association. Reprint 2025-26

India and the Contemporary World 112 The loss of the finest grazing lands and water resources created pressure on the small area of land that the Maasai were confined within. Continuous grazing within a small area inevitably meant a deterioration of the quality of pastures. Fodder was always in short supply. Feeding the cattle became a persistent problem. 3.2 The Borders are Closed In the nineteenth century, African pastoralists could move over vast areas in search of pastures. When the pastures were exhausted in one place they moved to a different area to graze their cattle. From the late nineteenth century, the colonial government began imposing various restrictions on their mobility. Like the Maasai, other pastoral groups were also forced to live within the confines of special reserves. The boundaries of these reserves became the limits within which they could now move. They were not allowed to move out with their stock without special permits. And it was difficult to get permits without trouble and harassment. Those found guilty of disobeying the rules were severely punished. Pastoralists were also not allowed to enter the markets in white areas. In many regions, they were prohibited from participating in any form of trade. White settlers and European colonists saw pastoralists as dangerous and savage – people with whom all contact had to be minimised. Cutting off all links was, however, never really possible, because white colonists had to depend on black labour to bore mines and, build roads and towns. The new territorial boundaries and restrictions imposed on them suddenly changed the lives of pastoralists. This adversely affected Source F In most places in colonial Africa, the police were given instructions to keep a watch on the movements of  pastoralists, and prevent them from entering white areas. The following is one such instruction given by a magistrate to the police, in south-west Africa, restricting the movements of the pastoralists of Kaokoland in Namibia: ‘Passes to enter the Territory should not be given to these Natives unless exceptional circumstances necessitate their entering … The object of the above proclamation is to restrict the number of natives entering the Territory and to keep a check on them, and ordinary visiting passes should therefore never be issued to them.’ ‘Kaokoveld permits to enter’, Magistrate to Police Station Commanders of Outjo and Kamanjab, 24 November, 1937. Source Reprint 2025-26

Pastoralists in the Modern World 113 both their pastoral and trading activities. Earlier, pastoralists not only looked after animal herds but traded in various products. The restrictions under colonial rule did not entirely stop their trading activities but they were now subject to various restrictions. 3.3 When Pastures Dry Drought affects the life of pastoralists everywhere. When rains fail and pastures are dry, cattle are likely to starve unless they can be moved to areas where forage is available. That is why, traditionally, pastoralists are nomadic; they move from place to place. This nomadism allows them to survive bad times and avoid crises. But from the colonial period, the Maasai were bound down to a fixed area, confined within a reserve, and prohibited from moving in search of pastures. They were cut off from the best grazing lands and forced to live within a semi-arid tract prone to frequent droughts. Since they could not shift their cattle to places where pastures were available, large numbers of Maasai cattle died of starvation and disease in these years of drought. An enquiry in 1930 showed that the Maasai in Kenya possessed 720,000 cattle, 820,000 sheep and 171,000 donkeys. In just two years of severe drought, 1933 and 1934, over half the cattle in the Maasai Reserve died. As the area of grazing lands shrank, the adverse effect of the droughts increased in intensity. The frequent bad years led to a steady decline of the animal stock of the pastoralists. 3.4 Not All were Equally Affected In Maasailand, as elsewhere in Africa, not all pastoralists were equally affected by the changes in the colonial period. In pre-colonial times Maasai society was divided into two social categories – elders and warriors. The elders formed the ruling group and met in periodic councils to decide on the affairs of the community and settle disputes. The warriors consisted of younger people, mainly responsible for the protection of the tribe. They defended the community and organised cattle raids. Raiding was important in a society where cattle was wealth. It is through raids that the power of different pastoral groups was asserted. Young men came to be recognised as members of the warrior class when they proved their manliness by raiding the cattle of other pastoral groups and participating in wars. They, however, were subject to the authority of the elders. Fig.16 – Note how the warriors wear traditional deep red shukas, brightly beaded Maasai jewelry and carry five-foot, steel tipped spears. Their long pleats of intricately plaited hair are tinted red with ochre. As per tradition they face East to honour the rising sun. Warriors are in charge of society's security while boys are responsible for herding livestock. During the drought season, both warriors and boys assume responsibility for herding livestock. Courtesy: The Massai Association. Reprint 2025-26

India and the Contemporary World 114 To administer the affairs of the Maasai, the British introduced a series of measures that had important implications. They appointed chiefs of different sub-groups of Maasai, who were made responsible for the affairs of the tribe. The British imposed various restrictions on raiding and warfare. Consequently, the traditional authority of both elders and warriors was adversely affected. The chiefs appointed by the colonial government often accumulated wealth over time. They had a regular income with which they could buy animals, goods and land. They lent money to poor neighbours who needed cash to pay taxes. Many of them began living in towns, and became involved in trade. Their wives and children stayed back in the villages to look after the animals. These chiefs managed to survive the devastations of war and drought. They had both pastoral and non-pastoral income, and could buy animals when their stock was depleted. But the life history of the poor pastoralists who depended only on their livestock was different. Most often, they did not have the resources to tide over bad times. In times of war and famine, they lost nearly everything. They had to go looking for work in the towns. Some eked out a living as charcoal burners, others did odd jobs. The lucky could get more regular work in road or building construction. The social changes in Maasai society occurred at two levels. First, the traditional difference based on age, between the elders Fig.17 - Even today, young men go through an elaborate ritual before they become warriors, although actually it is no longer common. They must travel throughout the section's region for about four months, ending with an event where they run to the homestead and enter with an attitude of a raider. During the ceremony, boys dress in loose clothing and dance non-stop throughout the day. This ceremony is the transition into a new age. Girls are not required to go through such a ritual. Courtesy: The Massai Association. Reprint 2025-26

Pastoralists in the Modern World 115 and warriors, was disturbed, though it did not break down entirely. Second, a new distinction between the wealthy and poor pastoralists developed. Conclusion So we see that pastoral communities in different parts of the world are affected  in a variety of different ways by changes in the modern world. New laws and new borders affect the patterns of their movement. With increasing restrictions on their mobility, pastoralists find it difficult to move in search of pastures. As pasture lands disappear grazing becomes a problem, while pastures that remain deteriorate through continuous over grazing. Times of drought become times of crises, when cattle die in large numbers. Yet, pastoralists do adapt to new times. They change the paths of their annual movement, reduce their cattle numbers, press for rights to enter new areas, exert political pressure on the government for relief, subsidy and other forms of support and demand a right in the management of forests and water resources. Pastoralists are not relics of the past. They are not people who have no place in the modern world. Environmentalists and economists have increasingly come to recognise that pastoral nomadism is a form of life that is perfectly suited to many hilly and dry regions of the world. Fig.18 – A Raika shepherd on Jaipur highway. Heavy traffic on highways has made migration of shepherds a new experience. Reprint 2025-26

India and the Contemporary World 116 Questions ? Activities 1. Explain why nomadic tribes need to move from one place to another. What are the advantages to the environment of this continuous movement? 2. Discuss why the colonial government in India brought in the following laws. Imagine that it is 1950 and you are a 60-year-old Raika herder living in post-Independence India. You are telling your grand-daughter about the changes which have taken place in your lifestyle after Independence. What would you say? 2. Imagine that you have been asked by a famous magazine to write an article about the life and customs of the Maasai in pre-colonial Africa. Write the article, giving it an interesting title. 3. content.content: Everything in the universe is made up of material which scientists have named matter. Matter occupies space and has mass. [cite: 9660] Early Indian philosophers classified matter into five basic elements: the 'Panch Tatva' (air, earth, fire, sky, and water). [cite: 9661]

content.subsection_heading: Matter is Made Up of Particles
content.content: For a long time, two schools of thought prevailed regarding the nature of matter: one believed matter to be continuous (like a block of wood), and the other believed it was made up of particles. [cite: 9665] Modern science confirms that matter is particulate. [cite: 9660]
Particles of matter have space between them [cite: 9669], are continuously moving (this movement increases with temperature) [cite: 9673], and attract each other. [cite: 9678]

Matter exists in three main states: Solid (definite shape, distinct boundaries, fixed volume, rigid) [cite: 9681], Liquid (no definite shape, fixed volume, takes the shape of the container) [cite: 9682], and Gas (highly compressible, no definite shape or volume). [cite: 9683]

* Melting Point: The temperature at which a solid converts to a liquid at atmospheric pressure. [cite: 9700] The energy supplied for this change (without temperature rise) is called the latent heat of fusion. [cite: 9703]
* Boiling Point: The temperature at which a liquid starts boiling to form a vapor at atmospheric pressure. [cite: 9706] The energy supplied for this change is called the latent heat of vaporisation. [cite: 9707]

* Sublimation: The change of state directly from solid to gas without passing through the liquid state (e.g., camphor, ammonium chloride). [cite: 9709]
* Evaporation: A surface phenomenon where liquid changes into vapor below its boiling point. [cite: 9718] Evaporation causes cooling. [cite: 9720]

content.chapter: Chapter 2: IS MATTER AROUND US PURE?
content.content: For a scientist, a pure substance means that all the constituent particles of that substance are the same in their chemical nature. A pure substance consists of a single type of particle. Most of the matter around us exists as mixtures of two or more pure components (e.g., sea water, minerals, soil). [cite: 15399, 15400]

content.chapter: Chapter 2: IS MATTER AROUND US PURE?
content.content:
* Homogeneous Mixtures (Solutions): Have a uniform composition throughout (e.g., salt dissolved in water, sugar solution, air). [cite: 15402, 15403]
* Heterogeneous Mixtures: Have a non-uniform composition; visible boundaries of separation (e.g., soil, oil and water, sodium chloride and iron filings). [cite: 15404]

content.chapter: Chapter 2: IS MATTER AROUND US PURE?
content.content: A solution is a homogeneous mixture of two or more substances. It consists of a solute (smaller amount) and a solvent (larger amount). The particles are smaller than 1 nm in diameter and do not show the Tyndall effect (scattering of a beam of light). [cite: 15408, 15410]

content.chapter: Chapter 2: IS MATTER AROUND US PURE?
content.content:
* Suspension: A heterogeneous mixture where the solute particles are visible and settle down when left undisturbed. [cite: 15412]
* Colloid: A heterogeneous mixture whose particles are big enough to scatter light (Tyndall effect) but are stable and do not settle down (e.g., milk, starch solution). [cite: 15415, 15416]

content.chapter: Chapter 2: IS MATTER AROUND US PURE?
content.section_heading: 2.3 Separating the Components of a Mixture
content.content: Common separation techniques include: Evaporation (for volatile solvent and non-volatile solute), Centrifugation (separating dense particles from a liquid, e.g., cream from milk), Sublimation (for components that sublime, e.g., camphor), Chromatography (separating colors in a dye), Distillation (separating miscible liquids with large boiling point difference), and Fractional Distillation (for miscible liquids with close boiling points). [cite: 15421, 15423, 15425, 15427, 15430, 15433]

content.chapter: Chapter 2: IS MATTER AROUND US PURE?
content.content:
* Physical Change: A change in physical properties (like state or color) without changing the chemical nature of the substance (e.g., freezing water, dissolving salt). [cite: 15436]
* Chemical Change: A change that results in a new substance with different chemical properties (e.g., rusting of iron, burning a candle). [cite: 15439]

content.chapter: Chapter 2: IS MATTER AROUND US PURE?
content.content:
* Element: A substance that cannot be broken down into simpler substances by chemical reactions (e.g., Sodium, Iron). [cite: 15443]
* Compound: A substance composed of two or more elements chemically combined in a fixed proportion (e.g., Water (H2O), Calcium Carbonate (CaCO3)). [cite: 15447]

Ancient philosophers, including India's Maharishi Kanad (who named the smallest particle Parmanu) and Greek philosophers Democritus and Leucippus (who called them atoms), hypothesized about the indivisibility of matter. [cite: 13233, 13235] Antoine L. Lavoisier laid the foundation of chemical sciences by establishing the laws of chemical combination. [cite: 13237]
The Law of Conservation of Mass states that mass can neither be created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction. [cite: 13239]

The Law of Constant Proportions (by Proust) states that in a chemical substance, the elements are always present in definite proportions by mass (e.g., the ratio of mass of hydrogen to oxygen in water is always 1:8). [cite: 13243, 13244]

John Dalton's theory proposed that atoms are indivisible particles that cannot be created or destroyed, and that atoms of the same element are identical in mass and properties. He also stated that atoms combine in the ratio of small whole numbers to form compounds. [cite: 13246, 13247, 13251, 13253]
The standard for the atomic mass unit (u) is exactly 1/12 the mass of one atom of the carbon-12 isotope. [cite: 13264]
Atoms of most elements cannot exist independently; they form molecules (groups of atoms held together by chemical bonds) and ions (charged particles). [cite: 13268]

Dalton's theory proposed atoms are indivisible, but later discoveries showed atoms contain smaller sub-atomic particles. [cite: 10130] The challenge was to explain how these particles are arranged within the atom. [cite: 10130]

* Electron: Discovered by J. J. Thomson. It is a negatively charged sub-atomic particle. [cite: 10137, 10140]
* Proton: Discovered by E. Goldstein using canal rays. It is a positively charged sub-atomic particle. [cite: 10141]

Thomson proposed that an atom is a uniform sphere of positive charge with electrons embedded in it, like seeds in a watermelon. The positive and negative charges are equal, making the atom electrically neutral. [cite: 10148]

Rutherford's experiment led to the discovery of the Nucleus. The model states that there is a tiny, dense, positively charged center (nucleus), and most of the atom is empty space. Electrons revolve around the nucleus. The main drawback was that orbiting electrons should lose energy and crash into the nucleus, making the atom unstable. [cite: 10158, 10161, 10164]
Bohr proposed that electrons revolve in specific discrete orbits (energy shells) and do not radiate energy while in these orbits, making the atom stable. [cite: 10167]

* Neutron: Discovered by J. Chadwick. It is a neutral particle located in the nucleus, with mass nearly equal to a proton. [cite: 10173]
* Atomic Number (Z): The number of protons in an atom, which determines the element's identity. [cite: 10182]
* Mass Number (A): The total number of protons and neutrons (nucleons) in the nucleus. [cite: 10185]

* Isotopes: Atoms of the same element that have the same atomic number (Z) but different mass numbers (A), due to a different number of neutrons (e.g., C-12, C-14). [cite: 10191]
* Isobars: Atoms of different elements that have different atomic numbers (Z) but the same mass number (A). [cite: 10196]

content.chapter: Chapter 5: THE FUNDAMENTAL UNIT OF LIFE
content.content: Robert Hooke observed cells in a slice of cork in 1665. The word 'cell' (from Latin for 'a little room') is still used to describe the fundamental units of living things. [cite: 10609, 10610]

content.chapter: Chapter 5: THE FUNDAMENTAL UNIT OF LIFE
content.section_heading: 5.1 What are Living Organisms Made Up of?
content.content: The Cell Theory states that all plants and animals are composed of cells, and the cell is the basic unit of life. All cells arise from pre-existing cells (proposed by Virchow). [cite: 10615, 10616]

content.chapter: Chapter 5: THE FUNDAMENTAL UNIT OF LIFE
content.content:
* Plasma Membrane: The outer covering of the cell, which is selectively permeable (regulates entry/exit of some substances). [cite: 10620]
* Osmosis: The movement of water through a selectively permeable membrane from a region of high water concentration to a region of low water concentration. [cite: 10624]

content.chapter: Chapter 5: THE FUNDAMENTAL UNIT OF LIFE
content.content:
* Cell Wall: A rigid, non-living outer layer found in plant cells that provides structural strength and protection. [cite: 10629]
* Nucleus: The 'brain' of the cell, containing chromosomes (genetic material: DNA) that control cell activities. [cite: 10634]
* Cytoplasm: The fluid substance inside the plasma membrane, containing specialized cell organelles. [cite: 10640]

content.chapter: Chapter 5: THE FUNDAMENTAL UNIT OF LIFE
content.content:
* Prokaryotic Cell: Lack a well-defined nucleus and membrane-bound organelles (e.g., bacteria). [cite: 10643]
* Eukaryotic Cell: Possess a well-defined nucleus and membrane-bound organelles (e.g., plant and animal cells). [cite: 10646]

content.chapter: Chapter 5: THE FUNDAMENTAL UNIT OF LIFE
content.content:
* Endoplasmic Reticulum (ER): Manufactures lipids and proteins. [cite: 10651]
* Mitochondria: The powerhouse of the cell; releases energy in the form of ATP. [cite: 10660]
* Plastids (in plants): Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll and are responsible for photosynthesis. [cite: 10664]
* Vacuoles: Storage sacs (water, sap, waste). Large central vacuole in plant cells provides turgidity. [cite: 10668]

A tissue is a group of cells that are similar in structure and/or work together to achieve a particular function. [cite: 14979] Multicellular organisms show division of labour, where specialized functions are carried out by specific tissues. [cite: 14976]

content.section_heading: 6.1 Are Plants and Animals Made of Same Types of Tissues?
content.content: Plant tissues are mostly supportive and often dead, as plants are stationary. Animal tissues are mostly living and require more energy, reflecting their mobility. [cite: 14980]

Meristematic tissue consists of actively dividing cells and is responsible for growth. It is classified as: Apical (growth in length, tips of stem/root), Lateral (growth in girth, cambium), and Intercalary (at the base of leaves/internodes). [cite: 14981, 14983, 14985]

Permanent tissues are derived from meristematic tissue but have lost the ability to divide. They are classified as: Simple Permanent Tissues (Parenchyma, Collenchyma, Sclerenchyma) and Complex Permanent Tissues (Xylem and Phloem). [cite: 14986, 14995]

* Xylem: Conducts water and minerals vertically from the roots to the plant parts. [cite: 14997]
* Phloem: Transports food (prepared in the leaves) to all parts of the plant. [cite: 14999]

Animal tissues are grouped into four main types: Epithelial (covering and protective), Connective (connecting various organs, e.g., blood, bone), Muscular (movement), and Nervous (transmitting messages). [cite: 15000]

Examples of connective tissue include: Blood (fluid matrix called plasma, transports), Bone (strong, supportive), Ligaments (connects bone to bone), Tendons (connects muscle to bone), Cartilage (smooths bone surfaces), Areolar (fills space inside organs), and Adipose (fat storage). [cite: 15002, 15004, 15006, 15008, 15010, 15011]

Muscular tissue is responsible for movement. The three types are: Striated (skeletal, voluntary control), Unstriated (smooth, involuntary control, in internal organs), and Cardiac (involuntary, unique to the heart, rhythmic contraction/relaxation). [cite: 15014, 15017, 15020]

The nervous tissue is composed of specialized cells called neurons that transmit stimuli rapidly. A neuron consists of a cell body, axon (long, single process), and dendrites (short, branched processes). [cite: 15023, 15024]

An object is perceived to be in motion when its position changes with time, relative to a reference point. Motion is relative; an object can be moving for one person and stationary for another. [cite: 16296, 16301]

Motion is described using a reference point (origin). Scalar Quantity has only magnitude (e.g., distance, speed). Vector Quantity has both magnitude and direction (e.g., displacement, velocity, acceleration). [cite: 16303]

Distance is the total path length covered by an object. Displacement is the shortest distance between the initial and final positions. Displacement can be zero, but distance can never be zero for a moving object. [cite: 16304]

* Uniform Motion: An object covers equal distances in equal intervals of time (constant speed). [cite: 16315]
* Non-Uniform Motion: An object covers unequal distances in equal intervals of time (changing speed). [cite: 16317]

* Speed: Distance traveled per unit time. Speed = Distance / Time. SI unit: m/s. [cite: 16318]
* Velocity: Speed of an object in a specific direction. Velocity = Displacement / Time. [cite: 16321]

Acceleration (a) is the rate of change of velocity: a = (v - u) / t where v is the final velocity, u is the initial velocity, and t is the time taken. Acceleration is a vector quantity, with the SI unit m s^-2. [cite: 16325, 16327]

* Distance-Time Graph: The slope of the graph represents the speed. [cite: 16333]
* Velocity-Time Graph: The slope represents acceleration, and the area under the graph represents the displacement. [cite: 16335, 16336]

The three equations that describe the motion of an object under uniform acceleration are:
(i) v = u + a t (velocity-time relation)
(ii) s = u t + 1/2 a t^2 (position-time relation)
(iii) 2 a s = v^2 - u^2 (position-velocity relation). [cite: 16346, 16347, 16348]

content.chapter: Chapter 8: FORCE AND LAWS OF MOTION
content.content: A force is based on the concept of a push, hit, or pull. We experience force as a muscular effort required to put a stationary object into motion or to stop a moving object. It is only explained by describing its effect on an object. [cite: 11252]

content.chapter: Chapter 8: FORCE AND LAWS OF MOTION
content.content: An unbalanced force is required to change the state of motion of an object. A Balanced Force can change the shape of an object but cannot cause motion. [cite: 11254]

content.chapter: Chapter 8: FORCE AND LAWS OF MOTION
content.content: An object remains in a state of rest or uniform motion in a straight line unless acted upon by an external unbalanced force. The natural tendency to resist a change in state of motion is called Inertia. Mass is the measure of inertia. [cite: 11261, 11257]

content.chapter: Chapter 8: FORCE AND LAWS OF MOTION
content.content:
* Momentum (p): The product of mass and velocity (p = m v). SI unit: kg m s^-1. [cite: 11269]
* The Second Law of Motion states that the rate of change of momentum of an object is proportional to the applied unbalanced force. Formula: F = m a. The SI unit of force is the newton (N). [cite: 11277, 11278]

content.chapter: Chapter 8: FORCE AND LAWS OF MOTION
content.content: To every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction. The action and reaction forces always act on two different objects. [cite: 11287]

content.chapter: Chapter 8: FORCE AND LAWS OF MOTION
content.content: The total momentum of two objects remains unchanged before and after a collision, provided no external unbalanced force acts on them (Total momentum before collision = Total momentum after collision). [cite: 11295]
The same force—the gravitational force—is responsible for objects falling towards the Earth, the Moon going around the Earth, and the planets revolving around the Sun. [cite: 12028, 12031]

Every object in the universe attracts every other object with a force (F) that is directly proportional to the product of their masses (m1, m2) and inversely proportional to the square of the distance (r) between them: F = G * (m1 * m2) / r^2. [cite: 12040] G is the Universal Gravitational Constant (6.673 x 10^-11 N m^2 kg^-2). [cite: 12041]

Free Fall is the motion of an object under the influence of gravity alone. The acceleration produced by the Earth's gravitational force is the acceleration due to gravity (g), with a value near the Earth's surface of g ≈ 9.8 m s^-2. [cite: 12047, 12053]

* Mass (m): The quantity of matter in an object, which remains constant everywhere. [cite: 12061]
* Weight (W): The force of gravity acting on an object (W = m g). Weight varies from place to place (e.g., lower on the Moon). [cite: 12062, 12066]

* Buoyancy: The upward force exerted by a fluid on a submerged object. [cite: 12076]
* Archimedes' Principle: An object immersed in a fluid experiences an upward force equal to the weight of the fluid displaced by it. This principle is used to determine if an object will float or sink. [cite: 12079, 12081]

All living beings and machines need food/fuel for energy to perform activities like playing, reading, lifting loads, or ploughing fields. Living beings have to perform life processes that require energy from food. [cite: 13676, 13677]

content.subsection_heading: 10.1.1 NOT MUCH 'WORK' IN SPITE OF WORKING HARD!
content.content: In science, little or no 'work' is done if there is no displacement of the object, even if a person is exhausted (e.g., pushing a rock that doesn't move or holding a heavy load still). [cite: 13685]
Two conditions must be met for work to be done in science: (i) a force must act on an object, and (ii) the object must be displaced. [cite: 13690]

content.subsection_heading: 10.1.3 WORK DONE BY A CONSTANT FORCE
content.content: When a constant force (F) displaces an object through a distance (s) in the direction of the force, the work done (W) is defined as the product of the force and the displacement: W = F s. [cite: 13693]

The SI unit of work is the joule (J), which is equivalent to one newton-metre (N m). One joule is the amount of work done when a force of 1 N displaces an object by 1 m in the direction of the force. [cite: 13697]
Energy is defined as the capacity to do work. The Sun is the biggest natural source of energy. [cite: 13702]

Kinetic energy (KE) is the energy possessed by an object due to its motion. It is expressed as: KE = 1/2 m v^2 where m is the mass and v is the velocity. The SI unit of energy is the joule (J). [cite: 13707, 13708, 13710]
Potential energy is the energy possessed by an object by virtue of its position or configuration (e.g., energy stored in a stretched rubber band). [cite: 13714]

content.section_heading: Potential Energy of an Object at a Height
content.content: The gravitational potential energy of an object of mass m raised to a height h is Ep = m g h. The work done by gravity depends only on the difference in vertical heights. [cite: 13716]

The Law of Conservation of Energy states that energy can only be converted from one form to another; it can neither be created nor destroyed. The total mechanical energy (sum of kinetic and potential energy) remains constant. [cite: 13725]
Power is the rate of doing work or the rate of transfer of energy. Mathematically, it is P = Work done / time taken. [cite: 13728, 13730]
The SI unit of power is the watt (W). One watt of power is defined as a rate of working of 1 J/s. The commercial unit of energy is the kilowatt hour (kWh). [cite: 13732, 13734]

Sound is a form of energy which produces the sensation of hearing in our ears. Like other forms of energy, sound obeys the law of conservation of energy (energy can neither be created nor destroyed). [cite: 13813]
Sound is produced by vibrating objects. A vibration is a rapid to-and-fro motion of an object. The human voice is produced by vibrations in the vocal cords. [cite: 13817, 13821]

Sound requires a medium (solid, liquid, or gas) to travel. Sound is transmitted as a disturbance, but the particles of the medium vibrate and do not travel all the way to the ear. [cite: 13826, 13829]

Sound travels as a longitudinal wave (a pressure or density variation). Regions of high pressure (high density of particles) are called Compressions (C), and regions of low pressure (low density of particles) are called Rarefactions (R). [cite: 13830, 13831]
Pitch is the property that distinguishes a shrill sound from a flat one. It is directly related to the frequency of the sound wave. Higher frequency means higher pitch. [cite: 13835]

Loudness is determined by the amplitude of the wave. A louder sound is associated with higher energy and the loudness is a physiological response of the ear to the intensity of the sound. [cite: 13836]

content.section_heading: Speed of Sound in Different Media
content.content: Sound travels fastest in solids, slower in liquids, and slowest in gases. For example, the speed of sound is 6420 m/s in Aluminium, 1498 m/s in distilled water, and 346 m/s in air (at 22°C). [cite: 13840, 13841]

Sound bounces off a solid or liquid surface and follows the same laws of reflection as light. The reflected sound heard a little later is called an echo. To hear a distinct echo, the time interval must be at least 0.1 s. [cite: 13845, 13846]

The audible range of sound for human beings extends from about 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz. Sounds of frequencies below 20 Hz are called infrasound and sounds above 20,000 Hz are called ultrasound. [cite: 13854, 13855]

Ultrasound is used for cleaning hard-to-reach parts, detecting cracks and flaws in metal blocks, medical imaging (e.g., echocardiography and ultrasound scanners), and in SONAR (Sound Navigation And Ranging) to measure distance, direction, and speed of objects underwater. [cite: 13856, 13859, 13861]

All living organisms need food, which supplies proteins, carbohydrates, fats, vitamins, and minerals for growth and health. Due to India's growing population, there is a need to increase production efficiency in agriculture and animal husbandry (Green and White Revolutions). [cite: 12617, 12625, 12627]

Goals for improvement include higher yield, good quality, biotic and abiotic resistance, and wider adaptability. Hybridization (crossing genetically dissimilar plants) is a primary method for variety improvement. [cite: 12631, 12634]

Management involves: Nutrient Management (supply of nutrients, manure, and fertilizers), Irrigation (supplying water), and Cropping Patterns such as Inter-cropping (growing two or more crops in definite rows) and Crop Rotation (growing different crops successively). [cite: 12638, 12642, 12646, 12648]

* Animal Husbandry: Scientific management of animal livestock (shelter, feeding, breeding, disease control). [cite: 12658]
* Cattle Farming: For milk (dairy) and draught work. Uses include increasing the length of the Lactation Period (milk-producing period). [cite: 12660]
* Poultry Farming: For egg (layers) and meat (broilers). Cross-breeding is done to enhance production. [cite: 12665]
* Fish Production: Includes Capture Fishing (natural resources) and Culture Fishery (farming). Composite Fish Culture is a common system. [cite: 12668, 12670]
Apiculture is the rearing of honey bees for honey and beeswax. Good quality honey is obtained by keeping bees in apiaries. [cite: 12674]
